Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Numbers 16:26–50, compiled from the sources available within the search limits.

---

## Numbers 16:26–50 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 26 — Moses warns the congregation to separate from the rebels

**Traditional reading:** Moses, acting on God’s command (v. 24), pleads with the people to distance themselves from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. The command not to “touch anything that belongs to them” signals that these men and their possessions were under the *ban* (Hebrew *ḥērem*), devoted to destruction. The Pulpit Commentary compares it to the case of Achan in Joshua 7:1 — to touch what is anathema is to share in the judgment. Gill notes that touching their goods would mean being “consumed in all their sins” — sharing both their guilt and their punishment. Whedon (Methodist) adds that voluntary separation from sinners under judgment is an act of protest against their wickedness and an acknowledgment of the justice of God’s punishment.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-26.htm (Pulpit)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/16.htm (Gill)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)

---

### v. 27 — The congregation moves away; Dathan and Abiram stand defiantly at their tents

**Traditional reading:** The people obey and move “from the dwellings of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.” Meanwhile, Dathan and Abiram come out with their wives, sons, and little children, standing at their tent doors in an attitude of defiance or curiosity — not repentance. Whedon comments that “their attitude was not that of penitence, but of curiosity or defiance. Earnest prayer might have saved them even then, but men abandoned by the grieved Spirit of God cannot pray.” Wesley’s Notes are closely parallel. The Pulpit Commentary notes that nothing is said of Korah here — he may have already been at the tabernacle with the 250 incense-offerers (see discussion at vv. 31–33). The presence of wives and children shows that whole families were swept into judgment through the head of the household’s sin.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/16.htm (Wesley)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/16.htm (Pulpit)

---

### v. 28 — Moses declares that the coming judgment will vindicate his divine commission

**Traditional reading:** Moses states that the coming event will prove that “the LORD has sent me” and that his actions were “not my own doing” (literally, “not of my heart”). The Pulpit Commentary emphasizes that Moses disclaims all self-seeking in his leadership. Constable (evangelical) notes that the point is that “rebellion against those whom Yahweh has chosen is rebellion against Him” — but this does not mean leaders are always right; it means that when God has appointed a leader, rebellion against that leader is rebellion against God. Enduring Word (Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic) stresses that Moses rested in God’s vindication rather than using his political power to arrest the rebels.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/16.htm (Pulpit)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/ (Enduring Word)

---

### v. 29 — The test: a natural death vs. a supernatural judgment

**Traditional reading:** Moses sets up a clear test. If Korah and his company die “the common death of all men” (Gill: “as every man dies”), then the LORD has not sent Moses. The phrase “visited after the visitation of all men” (Pulpit: the Hebrew *pāqad* can mean God’s providential oversight either for good or for judgment) means dying by any ordinary providential means. The logic is simple: only a supernatural, unmistakable judgment can prove divine commissioning.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/16.htm (Pulpit)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/16.htm (Gill)

---

### v. 30 — “If the LORD brings about something unprecedented” — a “new thing”

**Key phrase — “creates a new thing”:** The Hebrew is *bĕrî’â yibrā’* — literally “create a creation.” Whedon notes this means “do a thing never done before.” The earth opening to swallow them alive into Sheol would be unmistakably divine.

**Sheol:** Not “the pit” (as some translations render) but the realm of the dead. The Pulpit Commentary explains Sheol as Hades, the place of departed spirits, conceived (by the common instinct of mankind) as being “under the earth.” Constable cites G. Wenham: “Sheol, the abode of the dead, is pictured as lying immediately under the surface of the ground.” They would go down “alive” (*ḥayyîm*) — conscious and living, not dying first — directly into the realm of the dead.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/16.htm (Pulpit)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)

---

### vv. 31–33 — The earth swallows the rebels

**Traditional reading:** “As soon as Moses had finished speaking,” the ground split. The earth swallowed them, their households, all Korah’s men, and all their possessions. They “went down alive into Sheol” and “vanished from the assembly.”

**The fate of Korah himself — a debated question:** The Pulpit Commentary tackles a textual difficulty. Verse 32 says the earth swallowed “all Korah’s men” — but does not explicitly mention Korah himself. Numbers 26:10 seems to say Korah was swallowed; Deuteronomy 11:6 and Psalm 106:17 mention only Dathan and Abiram. The Pulpit Commentary concludes it is most probable that Korah had moved his dwelling near the Reubenites and was swallowed with them. Whedon takes a different view: that Korah, “with brazen brow, proceeded to burn incense with the insurgent princes, and was consumed with them by ‘a fire from the Lord.’” Constable notes that “the men who belonged to Korah” were apparently his followers, since some or all of his sons did not die (Numbers 26:11, 58; 1 Chronicles 6:18–22).

Gill does not resolve the question definitively but records the survival of Korah’s sons, who later became temple singers (the “sons of Korah” of the Psalms).
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/16.htm (Pulpit)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/ (Enduring Word/Guzik on Korah’s sons)

---

### v. 34 — Israel flees in terror

**Traditional reading:** “At their cries, all the people of Israel who were around them fled.” The Pulpit Commentary observes that the cries of the descending rebels were audible until the earth closed over them. Whedon notes that the people, who moments before had been sympathizers with the rebels, “instinctively flee from destruction.” This is not repentance but raw terror — “The earth may swallow us too!”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/16.htm (Pulpit)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)

---

### v. 35 — Fire consumes the 250 incense-offerers

**Traditional reading:** A separate judgment falls on the 250 men offering incense at the tabernacle. Fire “came forth from the LORD” — likely a lightning-like discharge from the glory-cloud (the Shekinah). Constable compares this to the judgment of Nadab and Abihu in Leviticus 10:2. Whedon notes that if the earth had swallowed these 250 as well, “Aaron and his sons and the tabernacle itself would have been in jeopardy,” so God used fire instead. Enduring Word (Guzik) observes that the two forms of judgment (earth swallowing and fire consuming) correspond to the two groups of rebels: the political challengers (Dathan, Abiram, and Korah’s household) and the religious challengers (the 250 would-be priests).
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/ (Enduring Word)

---

### vv. 36–38 — God commands that the censers be hammered into altar-covering

**Traditional reading:** The censers, though wielded by rebels, had been presented before the LORD and were therefore “holy.” Eleazar is told to remove them from the charred remains and scatter the coals far away (not on the holy altar). The bronze censers are to be hammered into sheets to overlay the altar of burnt offering.

Wesley’s Notes explain that the altar was made of wood overlaid with bronze (Exodus 27:1–2) before this time; this additional covering was “for farther ornament, and security against the fire, continually burning upon it.” Constable cites a modern scholar (Allen): “things are made holy in Scripture, not because people are holy, but because the things are presented to the Lord, who is holy.” The rebels “sinned at the cost of their own lives” (literally “sinned against their own souls,” as Gill and Whedon note).

**A denominational note — Wesley/Methodist:** Whedon (Methodist) draws a devotional application: “Every thing offered before the Lord is holy. Hence every soul consecrated to God is to account itself henceforth as holy and accepted by him, for he receives all that is offered to him in faith.” This reflects the Wesleyan emphasis on entire consecration.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/16.htm (Wesley)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/16.htm (Gill)

---

### vv. 39–40 — The memorial: no outsider may offer incense

**Traditional reading:** The bronze overlay becomes a permanent “sign” (memorial and warning) that “no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron should approach to offer incense before the LORD, lest he become like Korah and his followers.” Whedon calls it “a warning against grasping after priestly prerogatives,” and highlights the principle that God uses the punishment of the wicked as a deterrent for others. Constable agrees: “The Lord created another visual aid to remind the Israelites that offering incense was a ministry of the priests only.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)

---

### v. 41 — The next day: the whole congregation grumbles

**Traditional reading — the stunning blindness of the people:** Wesley exclaims, “Prodigious wickedness and madness so soon to forget such a terrible instance of Divine vengeance!” The people accuse Moses and Aaron: “You have killed the LORD’s people!” — calling the rebels whom God had just judged “the LORD’s people.” Whedon explains that they likely attributed the judgment to “some sort of magical incantation or mechanical contrivance on the part of Moses and Aaron” rather than to God. Constable adds that calling Korah’s company “the LORD’s people” shows they “failed to appreciate what it really meant to be His people.” Grant’s Commentary (evangelical) notes: “The people are often blinded by self-centeredness. They saw nothing but the work of the authorities in this catastrophic judgment.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/16.htm (Wesley)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/numbers-16.html (Grant)

---

### vv. 42–43 — The glory of the LORD appears; Moses and Aaron go before the Tabernacle

**Traditional reading:** As the mob gathers against them, Moses and Aaron turn toward the Tent of Meeting. Immediately the cloud covers it and the glory of the LORD appears. Wesley comments: “They — Moses and Aaron, who in all their distresses made God their refuge.” Constable notes that this is the second time in two days that the Shekinah glory appears in response to rebellion (cf. v. 19). Whedon describes it as “a supernatural resplendence flashed forth from the pillar of cloud premonitory of a stroke of judgment.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/16.htm (Wesley)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)

---

### vv. 44–45 — God threatens to consume the whole congregation; Moses and Aaron fall facedown

**Traditional reading:** God commands, “Get away from this congregation so that I may consume them in an instant.” Moses and Aaron do not move away; instead they fall facedown — an act of intercessory self-sacrifice. Whedon calls this “an act of heroic self-sacrifice equal to any in history,” noting that only the day before, the earth had swallowed those from whose tents people were told to separate. Now Moses and Aaron remain among the doomed people, “determined to avert consuming wrath or perish in the attempt.”

**A key difference from the earlier intercession (v. 22):** Constable, citing Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran/Reformed), explains why Moses did not intercede with words this time as he had before (Exodus 32:32; Numbers 14:13–19; 16:22). All his previous grounds of appeal were now exhausted: he could not stake his life for the nation because the nation had rejected him; he could not appeal to God’s honour among the heathen because God had already promised the earth would be filled with His glory; and he could not argue that only one man sinned, since the whole congregation had taken part with the rebels. There remained only one remedy: the divinely appointed high-priestly intercession through incense.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable, citing Keil & Delitzsch)

---

### v. 46 — Moses commands Aaron to make atonement with incense

**Traditional reading:** Moses, perceiving that the plague has already begun, tells Aaron to take his censer with fire from the altar, add incense, and “go quickly” to make atonement. Wesley comments: “Incense — Which was a sign of intercession, and was to be accompanied with it. … This he might do upon this extraordinary occasion, having God’s command for his warrant, though ordinarily incense was to be offered only in the tabernacle.”

**Atonement without blood — a significant point:** Whedon notes that “this is the only place where atonement is made without blood.” He explains that here the incense-offering “does not secure pardon, but only a reprieve; it shields the sinner from instant destruction and prolongs the forfeited lives.” Constable agrees: incense symbolizes prayer (cf. Exodus 30:8; Psalm 141:2; Luke 1:10; Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4), and Aaron was moving among the people interceding for them. The point is that the same instrument — a censer — that brought death when wielded by rebels (v. 35) brings life when wielded by God’s appointed priest.

**Reformed emphasis (Keil & Delitzsch, cited by Constable):** The incense-offering worked not because of Aaron’s subjective faith or sincerity but because of “the objective force of the divine appointment” — the high-priestly office itself carried God-given efficacy.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/16.htm (Wesley)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-16.html (Whedon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)

---

### vv. 47–48 — Aaron runs into the assembly; stands between the dead and the living

**Traditional reading:** Aaron, though about a hundred years old, “ran into the midst of the assembly.” He offered incense and made atonement. “He stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was halted.” Wesley suggests the plague moved in an orderly fashion from one end of the camp to the other, which allowed Aaron to position himself at the boundary between the already-stricken and the still-living.

**The Spurgeon sermon (Baptist/Reformed Baptist):** Charles Spurgeon preached on these verses on October 21, 1860, viewing Aaron as a type of Christ in five ways: (1) as the **Lover** of the people — Aaron interceded for the very people who had accused him, just as Christ loved those who dishonored Him; (2) as the **Mediator** — Aaron stood between the living and the dead; (3) as the **Priest** — using the censer that in rebel hands brought death but in appointed hands brought life; (4) the **Runner** — Aaron’s haste pictures Christ’s eagerness to save; (5) the **Accepted Intercessor** — the incense was received and the plague stopped. Spurgeon’s central point is that “Aaron … is a most magnificent picture of the Lord Jesus.” (Spurgeon sermon excerpt preserved at StudyLight.org.)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/numbers-16.html (Spurgeon)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/16.htm (Wesley)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/ (Enduring Word — also notes the incense = prayer symbolism, Christ as intercessor)

---

### v. 49 — 14,700 died, besides those who died in the Korah incident

**Traditional reading:** The death toll from the plague was 14,700, in addition to those who died in the earth-swallowing and the fire (the “matter of Korah”). Constable calls this “a divine judgment involving sudden death.” Enduring Word (Guzik) contextualises the number: “This is a large number, but not compared to the consuming of the whole nation. This was another step in the passing of the generation of unbelief in the wilderness, so a new generation of faith and boldness could be raised up to take the Promised Land.” No commentator treats the number as symbolic; all read it literally.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html (Constable)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/ (Enduring Word)

---

### v. 50 — Aaron returns to Moses; the plague has halted

**Traditional reading:** The verse provides a quiet, conclusive close. Aaron returns to Moses at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. The repetition of “the plague had been halted” (already stated in v. 48) underscores the finality of the atonement. Whedon and Wesley offer no separate note on this verse, treating it as the narrative conclusion. Grant’s Commentary draws the application: “This is another illustration of the intercessory grace of the Lord Jesus, our great high Priest, who preserves His people even from the deserved results of their own folly.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/numbers-16.html (Grant)

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Distinctives

**Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill):** Spurgeon reads the passage Christologically — Aaron as a type of Christ the Great High Priest who stands between the living and the dead. Gill provides meticulous Hebrew and rabbinic detail without pressing typology as far as Spurgeon. Both affirm the historicity of the judgment and the exclusive Aaronic priesthood as God-ordained.

**Methodist/Wesleyan (Wesley, Whedon):** Wesley treats the passage with emphasis on practical holiness and the danger of rebellion against divinely appointed authority. Whedon stresses the moral and spiritual dimensions: the people’s “spiritual stupidity,” Aaron’s “spirit of forgiveness,” and the principle of entire consecration. Whedon also makes the distinctive comment (reflecting Methodist anti-sacerdotalism) that “Protestantism, having no priest but Jesus Christ, is well guarded against this evil [of ambitious men seeking priestly power].”

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Guzik emphasises intercessory prayer as modelled by Aaron: “Intercessors do the same thing today; they stand between the dead and the living, begging for God’s mercy, preserving and promoting life with their prayer.” The application is immediate and practical for Christian life, with less attention to historical-critical detail.

**Lutheran/Reformed (Keil & Delitzsch, cited by Constable):** The emphasis falls on the *objective* efficacy of the divinely appointed means — the incense worked because of God’s institution, not because of Aaron’s subjective faith. This reflects a sacramental understanding of divinely given means of grace.

**Evangelical (Constable):** Constable synthesises from multiple sources (Ashley, Wenham, Allen, Keil & Delitzsch) with a focus on the narrative’s theological message: the legitimacy of the Aaronic priesthood, the seriousness of rebellion against God-appointed leaders, and the typological foreshadowing of Christ’s intercession.

**Older Anglican (Pulpit Commentary):** Provides detailed textual, lexical, and historical notes, carefully weighing the question of Korah’s fate, the meaning of *Sheol*, and the nature of the “plague,” with cautious conclusions.
